questions.prompt: Explain how the event loop decides the order in which synchronous code, promise callbacks and timers run.

keyPoints.text: Nothing asynchronous runs until the current synchronous code has finished.
keyPoints.quote: Call stack must empty before any async callback runs.

keyPoints.text: Promise callbacks are microtasks that run after the current script, ahead of rendering and the next macrotask.
keyPoints.quote: Microtasks (promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) run after current script but before rendering and next macrotask.

keyPoints.text: Timers, intervals, I/O and UI events are macrotasks.
keyPoints.quote: Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events.

keyPoints.text: The classic example therefore prints the two synchronous logs first, then the promise, then the timer.
The whole microtask queue drains before any further macrotask starts.
keyPoints.quote: All microtasks finish before the next macrotask.

keyPoints.text: requestAnimationFrame callbacks sit just before paint, after microtasks.
keyPoints.quote: requestAnimationFrame runs before paint, after microtasks.

questions.prompt: Why can scheduling work on the wrong queue freeze a page, and how should heavy work be split?

keyPoints.text: A long chain of microtasks can block rendering just like synchronous work.
keyPoints.quote: Long-running microtask (e.g. many chained .then) can block rendering.

keyPoints.text: The chunked processor reschedules itself with queueMicrotask, but the file notes requestAnimationFrame is the better yield point.
Putting heavy work in microtasks blocks the main thread.
keyPoints.quote: Blocking the main thread with heavy work in microtasks

keyPoints.text: A zero-delay timeout is still a queued macrotask, not an immediate call.
Scheduling too many microtasks starves the UI of a chance to update.
keyPoints.quote: Starving the UI by scheduling too many microtasks

keyPoints.text: Knowing which queue each primitive uses is what lets you fix UI jank by choosing the right one.
keyPoints.quote: Knowing the queues lets you choose the right scheduling primitive.

questions.prompt: How do the lab's async utilities rely on these scheduling rules to stay correct?

keyPoints.text: withTimeout races the work against a timer and clears the timer whichever side wins, so no stray macrotask is left pending.
concurrencyLimit workers claim an index synchronously before awaiting, because other workers run while one is suspended.
Results are written by index so input order survives tasks finishing in any order.
debounceAsync rejects the superseded call's promise so its caller never hangs on a cleared timer.
The task queue starts each task inside a promise chain and frees its slot in finally, so a throwing task cannot wedge the queue.
